title: Paralyzed Veterans of America v. D.C. Arena L.P. (1997)
shortTitle: Paralyzed Veterans of America v. D.C. Arena L.P. (1997)
summary: An agency's interpretation of its own ambiguous regulation, set out in a technical manual, receives deference and needs no notice and comment, but an agency may not change an authoritatively adopted interpretation of a regulation without notice and comment.
notes:
Key line: "It is certainly not open to an agency to promulgate mush and then give it concrete form only through subsequent less formal \"interpretations.\"" (Silberman, J.)

Citation: 117 F.3d 579 (D.C. Cir. 1997).

sections.Parties: The appellees and cross appellants were the Paralyzed Veterans of America and several Washington area sports fans who use wheelchairs. The appellants and cross appellees were D.C. Arena L.P., a District of Columbia limited partnership, and related entities that owned and would operate the MCI Center, an arena then under construction in downtown Washington to house the NBA's Washington Wizards and the NHL's Washington Capitals. The United States Department of Justice, which had declined repeated invitations from the district judge to intervene, participated only as amicus curiae in the district court and on appeal.
sections.Material Facts: Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act requires new public accommodations to be readily accessible and directs the Department of Justice to issue standards consistent with Access Board guidelines. Standard 4.33.3, adopted by Justice in July 1991 from the Board's guideline, requires wheelchair areas to provide lines of sight comparable to those for members of the general public. The Board's January 1991 proposal had acknowledged that this wording might not suffice where audiences frequently stand and deferred the standing spectator issue to later guidelines; Justice's statement of basis and purpose said nothing about it. In 1992 a mid level Justice official told stadium operators there was no such requirement, but in December 1994 it published, without notice and comment, a supplement to its Technical Assistance Manual requiring sightlines over standing spectators. A month later the arena owners, aware of Justice's position, chose seating bowls in which some but not all wheelchair seats had such sightlines.
sections.Procedural History: The Paralyzed Veterans and the individual plaintiffs sued the arena owners in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia under the ADA's private right of action, challenging the seating designs for lack of integration, dispersal and sightlines. The district judge found the seating adequately integrated but not adequately dispersed, deferred to Justice's manual interpretation as binding, and held that substantial compliance sufficed, approving a plan giving sightlines over standing spectators to 78 percent of wheelchair seats in one configuration and 85 to 88 percent in the other three. He refused to accept a second amicus brief from Justice. Both sides appealed. The D.C. Circuit heard argument on May 9, 1997, before Chief Judge Edwards and Judges Silberman and Sentelle, and on July 1, 1997, affirmed in an opinion by Judge Silberman.
sections.Issue: Whether the phrase lines of sight comparable to those for members of the general public in Standard 4.33.3 can bear the Department of Justice's interpretation requiring sightlines over standing spectators; whether that interpretation, announced in a technical assistance manual, is entitled to deference even though the Access Board drafted the language and Justice has no adjudicatory authority; whether the manual interpretation was a change from an earlier authoritative interpretation or a substantive rule, either of which would require notice and comment under 5 U.S.C. section 553; and whether the district court erred in requiring only substantial rather than complete compliance.
sections.Holding: The court held that the regulation was ambiguous as applied to standing spectators but easily read to require an unobstructed view, that Justice's interpretation was entitled to deference because Congress delegated to Justice the authority to issue and administer the standards and to publish technical manuals refining them, and that the interpretation was permissible. It held that an agency may not make a fundamental change in its interpretation of a substantive regulation without notice and comment, but that Justice had never authoritatively adopted a contrary position, since a speech by a mid level official was not a fair and considered departmental judgment. The manual interpretation was interpretive rather than substantive because it was drawn from the actual meaning of the regulation's words. The court affirmed the district court's discretion to require substantial compliance.
sections.Reasoning: Judge Silberman explained that deference to an agency's interpretation of its own regulation, rests on the agency's statutory role as sponsor of the regulation, not on drafting expertise, so it did not matter that the Access Board wrote the words; once Justice promulgated them they became Justice's responsibility. The court set an outer limit: a substantive regulation must have enough content to be a meaningful exercise in lawmaking, and an agency may not promulgate mush and give it concrete form only through later informal interpretations, because that would circumvent section 553. On change of position, the court rejected the government's analogy to Chevron: because the APA requires notice and comment for amendments of regulations, allowing a fundamental reinterpretation without those procedures would undermine the statute. But Justice's statement of basis and purpose never adopted the Board's reservation, the 1992 speech by a mid level official was not authoritative, and the owners knew of the manual before designing the arena. Whether an interpretation is substantive turns on how tightly it is drawn from the language of the rule; the government could have enforced the regulation itself without the manual, so the interpretation was not sufficiently additive to require notice and comment. Because the manual never said every wheelchair seat needed such a sightline, the district judge sitting in equity could require substantial compliance.
